title: How do speech therapy trainees experience encounters with seriously ill patients during their internship at the clinic?
summary:
Background
The care of increasingly multimorbid and critically ill patients in hospitals and on rehabilitation wards requires the integration of palliative knowledge, skills, and attitudes into clinical structures. This process presents challenges for staff who have previously provided purely curative care. Trainees in the therapeutic sector, such as speech therapists, occupational therapists, or physiotherapists, in particular, may be unprepared when confronted with dying patients during clinical internships. 
This study is dealing with the working conditions of speech therapists.

Speech therapists work as speech and language therapists in speech therapy practices or hospitals. They treat language, speech, and swallowing disorders in people of all ages. Speech therapy work in a hospital setting is often unfamiliar and, unlike working with children, involves dealing with seriously ill patients. Patients' speech and swallowing deteriorate particularly after strokes, periods of ventilation, chronic illnesses, and at the end of life. This is where speech and language therapists can help. Speech therapists require a three-year training program and sometimes additional study. In addition to theoretical knowledge, practical experience is also part of the training. This is carried out in a speech and language therapy practice or a hospital. Many speech and language therapists choose to complete an internship in a practice because they find working in a hospital difficult or feel overwhelmed. Those trainees who complete their internship in a hospital require a special level of support and guidance. The question is what this support might look like in concrete terms and where trainees would like practical and emotional support. To answer this question, up to 20 trainees in Hamburg and northern Germany will be interviewed. The trainees will be asked to report on their experiences during their internship in a hospital. They will be allowed to talk about what they did well and where they felt uncomfortable. They will be asked whether patients may have died and whether they were able to support seriously ill people, for example, through good oral care, respiratory therapy, or speech therapy. The interviews will be transcribed, and all personal elements such as names or ages will be deleted. The study director will compare the various interviews and try to identify common themes. Information will be collected on where speech therapy was able to support the trainees and where the trainees learned new things. In addition, individual points will be collected for the supervisors during the internships to give them tips on what they should pay attention to. The goal is for interns to feel comfortable in a hospital and to be able to provide holistic support to seriously ill people in their future professional lives in a speech therapy practice, during home visits, or in a hospital.
conditions: Critically ill patients often suffer from dyspnea and severe pain, making it impossible to swallow or speak. This results in dysphagia, xerostomia, loss of appetite, nausea, malnutrition with weight loss, increasing weakness, and communication difficulties. Speech therapists can improve quality of life through targeted therapy until the end of life. Learning this requires practical experience and knowledge of palliative treatment options in speech therapy. Even during speech therapist training, a foundation can be laid through theory and practice so that patients with severe illnesses can receive holistic support through palliative speech therapy.

interventions.name: Non-interventional study; open exploration of how speech therapy trainees experience encounters with serioulslyill patients in clinical internships. A minimum of 6 and a maximum of 20 semi-structured guided interviews of max. 60 minutes each will be conducted.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
• Speech therapists in their first to third year of training
• Speech therapists in their first or second degree
• Speech therapists in dual study programs
• Speech therapists who graduated no more than six months ago
• Training in accordance with the Speech Therapist Profession Act (LogopG) and the Training and Examination Regulations (LogAPrO)
• An internship of more than four weeks in an acute care or rehabilitation clinic at various locations (e.g., neurology, geriatrics, rehabilitation clinic)
• Experience working with critically ill patients during the internship and in various challenging and positive situations
• confident written and spoken German skills
Exclusion criteria:
Trainees who were accompanied by the applicant as a supervisor in the clinic during their external internship
